newsitem.title: UK: Sterling seen stalling at big Labour vote boost.
newsitem.headline: Sterling seen stalling at big Labour vote boost.

text.p: Sterling markets should embrace a victory for Britain's opposition Labour Party at a key parliamentary by-election this week, although a landslide win could unsettle the currency, analysts said on Wednesday.

Voters from the Wirral South constiutency in the north of England go to the polls on Thursday and are expected to hand victory to Labour, forcing the Conservative government into a minority Parliament.
"Markets are expecting the Labour Party to win. The leads from the latest opinion polls suggest it could be a landslide," said Gerard Lyons, chief economist at DKB International.

But a sweeping Labour victory at Wirral, while allaying fears of a hung Parliament, could knock sterling off its perch by raising the possibility of a landslide Labour win at the general election that which must be held by late May, analysts said.

"A hung Parliament isn't particularly a positive factor for the market because of the uncertainty that yields, nor is a landslide Labour victory because of the prospects...The markets may conclude it gives Labour a mandate for a more radical strategy," said Francis Breedon, senior foreign exchange economist at Lehman Brothers.
Analysts said a landslide win would give centre-left Labour, out of government since 1979, a mandate to be tougher on economic policy.

"I don't think the market is going to be pleased to see a landslide Labour victory at the general election. This is a party that has been out of office for 18 years," said Avinash Persaud, head of currency research at J.P. Morgan.

Although victory for Tony Blair's Labour Party at the Wirral by-election, made necessary by the death of the Conservative incumbent, could dent currency market sentiment, the impact will probably be short-lived.

"Whatever majority Blair gets isn't really going to affect Labour's macro-economic frame-work, which is pretty much in line with that of the Conservatives," said Paul Meggyesi, senior currency economist at Deutsche Morgan Grenfell.
A perky pound, which has climbed some 16 percent against a basket of major trading currencies since January, could also prove a boon after the general election.
Trading at 2.74 marks on Wednesday against 2.59 in early January, the strong pound will help keep inflation under control so that interest rates do not rise so sharply, economists said.
"Sterling so far has been good news for monetary policy...It has managed to fill in a hole left in by a rather lax policy in the run-up to the election," Breedon said.
And while a strong pound makes it harder for British exporters to sell their goods, economists say Labour will also have to focus on Britian's homeowners with mortgages.
"If Labour has a landslide it will give them more room to prove their toughness to the markets...But even so, Chancellor Brown would not need to raise rates by more than half a percent," said Lyons.
